p: Every morning at five o'clock, Awa hears the same sound. Vroom, vroom, cough, cough. It is her father's orange taxi, starting in front of the house in Abobo. The old car is tired, but it always starts. "Like me," her father says with a laugh.

Her father is called Moussa Traoré. He drives a woro-woro, a shared taxi, in Abidjan. He goes from Abobo to Adjamé, from Adjamé to Plateau, from Plateau to Cocody, all day long. He knows every street, every hole in the road, every seller at every corner. People in the neighbourhood call him "Vieux Père GPS", because he never gets lost.

Awa is fifteen. She is in *troisième*, her last year before high school. She is the best in her class in science. When she grows up, she wants to be a doctor. Not just any doctor: a doctor in a hospital for children, with a white coat and a stethoscope around her neck.

Her mother, Mariam, sells pagnes at the Abobo market. Her little brother, Ismaël, is eight. He has a big smile with no front teeth, and he wants to be a footballer, a pilot and a taxi driver, all at the same time.
The house is small: two rooms, a little courtyard with a mango tree, and a kitchen outside. But it is always full of noise, laughter and the smell of garba from the corner shop.
That Monday, at school, Madame Koné, the director, calls Awa into her office.
"Awa, sit down, please."
Awa sits. Her heart is beating fast. Did she do something wrong?

"You are one of our best students," says Madame Koné. "But your family has not paid the school fees for this term. Sixty-five thousand francs. If the money is not paid in one month, I'm afraid you cannot take the exam."

Awa looks at her hands. She knows. She has heard her parents talking at night, in low voices, when they think she is asleep. The taxi is getting old. Every week, something breaks. The market is slow this year.
"I understand, Madame," she says quietly.
"I'm sorry, my child. I really am."
That evening, at dinner, Awa doesn't eat much. Her father notices.
"What is it, my doctor?" He always calls her that. *My doctor.*
Awa hesitates. Then she tells them about Madame Koné, the sixty-five thousand francs, the one month.
Nobody speaks. Her mother puts down her spoon. Her father looks at the mango tree in the dark courtyard. Ismaël looks from one face to the other, not understanding.
"We will find the money," says her father finally. "Don't worry. Your job is to study."
But Awa sees the lines on his forehead. She sees her mother's tired eyes. And that night, in bed, she makes a decision.
The next morning, at five o'clock, when the orange taxi coughs in front of the house, Awa is already dressed and waiting by the door.
"Papa," she says. "On Saturday, I'm coming with you."
Her father laughed when she said it. "In the taxi? A taxi is not a place for a future doctor."
"Please, Papa. I can help. I can count the money. I can call the passengers. On weekends, you always say you need an *apprenti*."
He looked at her for a long time. Then he looked at her mother. Her mother shrugged, a small smile on her lips. "She has your head, Moussa. Hard like a stone."
"OK," he said at last. "Saturday. Five o'clock. Don't be late. And on Sunday, you study."

So on Saturday, Awa sits in the front seat. The sun is not up yet, but the streets are already full of people. Women carry big bowls of bananas on their heads. Men drink coffee in small plastic cups. Children run to the bus station with their school bags. The air smells of smoke, petrol and fried plantain.
"Adjamé! Adjamé! Plateau!" Awa shouts from the window. Her voice is small at first. Her father laughs.
"Louder! Nobody can hear a mouse!"
"ADJAMÉ! PLATEAU!"

The taxi fills up quickly. A student with a big bag. An old woman with a chicken in a basket. A man in a grey suit, talking on two phones at the same time. A young nurse in a blue uniform, with tired eyes.
"How much to Plateau, little girl?" asks the man in the suit.
"Three hundred francs, sir."
He gives her a thousand-franc note. She gives him seven hundred francs back, fast and correct, without counting on her fingers. Her father looks at her in the mirror and nods. He is proud.
At Adjamé, the traffic is terrible. Hundreds of taxis, buses, motorbikes and carts, all trying to pass at the same time. Everybody honks. A policeman blows his whistle, but nobody listens.
Next to them, a green taxi pushes in front. The driver is a big man with gold teeth. He shouts through the window.
"Hey, Moussa! Your old orange tomato is still alive? I thought it was dead last week!"
"Zié," her father says calmly, "my tomato is old, but it is honest."
Zié laughs and drives away, taking two of the passengers who were waiting for them.
"Who is he?" asks Awa.

"Zié. He has three taxis now. Young drivers work for him. He drives fast, he takes passengers from other drivers, and he gives money to the police so they don't stop him." Her father shakes his head. "Many people think he is clever."
"And you? What do you think?"
Her father is quiet for a moment. "I think a man must be able to sleep at night."
All day, they drive. Abobo, Adjamé, Plateau, Adjamé, Cocody, Adjamé, Abobo. Awa's voice becomes tired. Her back hurts. The seat is hot. But she learns many things.

She learns the price of every trip. She learns which corners have many passengers in the morning and which ones in the evening. She learns that you must never put a passenger with a big bag of fish next to a man in a white shirt.
At noon, they stop to eat attiéké and fish at a small maquis under a tree. Her father counts the money on the table. He counts slowly, two times.
"Eleven thousand five hundred," he says. "On a normal Saturday, I make eight thousand." He smiles at her. "You bring luck, Awa."

But Awa does the calculation in her head. Petrol: five thousand. The daily payment for the taxi owner: no, the taxi is theirs. Repairs: always. Sixty-five thousand francs in one month... She would need many, many Saturdays.
She doesn't say anything. She just eats her fish and smiles back at her father.
On the second Saturday, Awa brings a small green notebook.
"What is that for?" asks her father. "Are you going to do your homework in my taxi?"
"No, Papa. It's for the passengers."
She doesn't explain more. But all day, between two shouts of "Adjamé! Plateau!", she writes small notes. Not names. Just stories.

*The old woman with the chicken. Mama Akissi. She goes to Plateau every Saturday to see her daughter, who works in a bank. The chicken is a gift. Every week, a new chicken. "My daughter never cooks," she says. "So I cook for her, even from far away."*
*The student with the big bag. Kader. He studies engineering at the university in Cocody. He wants to build bridges. "Abidjan needs more bridges," he says. "Too many people, not enough roads."*
*The man with two phones. He sells telephones. He talks on two phones because he is selling to two people at the same time.*
In the evening, at home, Awa reads her notes to Ismaël. He laughs at the man with two phones. He asks questions about the chicken.
"Did the chicken know it was going to be eaten?"
"I don't think so."
"Poor chicken."
Her mother listens from the kitchen. "Why do you write all that, Awa?"

Awa thinks. "Because in the taxi, people are only passengers. Three hundred francs. Get in, get out. But they all have a life. A doctor must listen to people, no? Not only look at their bodies. Listen to their stories."
Her mother looks at her with a strange expression. Then she goes back to her pot. But Awa sees that she is smiling.
On the third Saturday, the young nurse in the blue uniform gets in the taxi again. She sits in the back, behind Awa. She looks very tired.
"Long night?" asks Awa.
The nurse is surprised. Passengers don't usually talk to her. "Very long. Twelve hours at the children's hospital in Cocody. Three new babies, one very sick little boy."
"Is he going to be OK?"
The nurse smiles for the first time. "Yes. I think so. He's strong."
Awa turns around in her seat. "I want to work in a children's hospital too. As a doctor."
"Really?" The nurse looks at her with new interest. "What's your name?"
"Awa. Awa Traoré."

"I'm Aminata. Listen, Awa. It's a long road. Many years of study. It's hard, and it's expensive. But it's the most beautiful job in the world." She takes a pen and writes something on a small piece of paper. "Here. My number. If you ever have questions about science, or about the job, call me."
Awa holds the paper like a treasure. When Aminata gets out at Cocody, Awa watches her walk to the hospital in her blue uniform until she disappears.
That evening, she writes in her notebook:
*Aminata. Nurse. Twelve hours of work, and she still smiles. One day, I want to work next to her.*
But that same evening, there is bad news. Her father counts the money for the week. Then he counts what is left after the petrol and the repairs.
"Twenty-two thousand," he says quietly to her mother, when he thinks Awa can't hear. "We have saved twenty-two thousand. And only two weeks left."
Awa lies in bed in the dark. Forty-three thousand francs more. In two weeks.
Through the window, she can see the old orange taxi under the mango tree. It looks like a tired animal, sleeping.
On Wednesday afternoon, Awa is in class when her phone vibrates in her bag. A message from her mother.
*Papa had a problem with the taxi. He is at Bakary's garage. Come after school.*

Bakary's garage is not really a garage. It is a piece of land between two buildings, full of old cars, tyres and oil on the ground. Bakary is a small, thin man with black hands and a radio that always plays zouglou.
When Awa arrives, the orange taxi is there, with its front open like a mouth. Her father is sitting on an old tyre. He looks older than this morning.
"What happened?"
"The engine," says Bakary, coming out from under the car. "The gearbox is finished. Completely finished, my sister. I can repair it, but I need new pieces. From Japan, or from Nigeria."
"How much?" asks her father.
Bakary wipes his hands on a red cloth. He doesn't want to say it. "A hundred and fifty thousand. Maybe a hundred and forty, if I find the pieces second-hand."
Nobody speaks. The radio plays a happy song. It sounds terrible.
On the way home, they walk. There is no taxi now. Her father walks slowly, his hands behind his back.
"Papa, what are we going to do?"
"Zié came to the garage," he says. "He wants to buy the taxi. Two hundred thousand francs, like this, broken. He will repair it and give it to one of his young drivers."
Awa stops walking. "And you? What will you do?"

"I can work for him. Drive one of his taxis. He keeps most of the money, I keep a little." He tries to smile. "With two hundred thousand, we pay your school, we pay the rent, and we keep a little for Ismaël."
"But it's *your* taxi, Papa. You bought it with twelve years of work. You told me."
He doesn't answer.
That night, Awa cannot sleep. She hears her parents talking in the other room.
"Moussa, you can't work for Zié. You know how he is."
"What can I do, Mariam? I have no taxi. The children must eat. Awa must take her exam."
"We will find another way."
"Which way?" His voice is tired, not angry. Only tired. "Tell me which way, and I will take it."
Silence.

Awa opens her green notebook under the blanket, with the light of her phone. She reads the stories of the passengers. Mama Akissi and her chickens. Kader and his bridges. Aminata and her twelve hours. All these people who work so hard, who don't give up.
Then she writes:
*Papa says a man must be able to sleep at night. Tonight, nobody in this house is sleeping.*

The next three days are difficult. Her father goes out every morning to look for work. He comes back in the evening with nothing. Her mother stays longer at the market, but the market is slow. Ismaël asks every day: "When is the orange taxi coming back?"
At school, Awa cannot concentrate. In the mathematics test on Friday, she gets eleven out of twenty. It is her worst mark of the year.
Her teacher, Monsieur Bamba, gives her the paper with a worried face. "Awa, what is happening? This isn't you."
"Nothing, Monsieur. I'm just tired."
He looks at her for a moment. "If you need to talk, my door is open."
She nods and puts the paper in her bag quickly, so nobody can see it.
On Saturday morning, there is no orange taxi coughing in front of the house. But at seven o'clock, Bakary calls.
"Moussa! I found the pieces. Second-hand, from a car in Yopougon. A hundred and thirty thousand. And for you, my brother, you can pay me a little every month."
Her father closes his eyes. "Thank you, Bakary. Thank you."
The taxi will drive again on Monday. But the school fees are still not paid. And now there is a debt.
On Monday, the orange taxi starts again. Vroom, vroom, cough, cough. It coughs a little less than before. Ismaël runs around it in the courtyard, shouting "It's alive! It's alive!"
The next Saturday, Awa is back in the front seat. Only one week left before the deadline. The family has saved thirty-one thousand francs. It is not enough.

It is a hot, busy day. In the afternoon, a young man gets in at Adjamé. He is well dressed, with expensive shoes and a black leather bag. He talks on the phone all the time, very fast, in French and in English.
"Yes, I'm coming. Yes, I have the money for the workers. No, Papa, I'm not late. OK, OK, I'm almost there."
At Cocody, near the big roundabout, he jumps out of the taxi. He throws a coin to Awa without looking, and he runs, still talking on the phone.
The taxi starts again. Two streets later, Awa turns around to count the passengers. And she sees it.
On the back seat, there is a black leather bag.
"Papa! He forgot his bag!"
Her father stops the car on the side of the road. The other passengers get out — they have arrived. Now there is only Awa and her father in the orange taxi.
Awa opens the bag. Inside, there are papers, a laptop, a phone charger. And a big brown envelope.
She opens the envelope.
Money. A lot of money. Bundles of ten-thousand-franc notes, held together with rubber bands. She has never seen so much money in her life.
Her father takes the envelope. He counts the bundles, his fingers shaking a little. "Ten bundles. Each bundle, five hundred thousand francs." He looks at her. "Five million francs, Awa."
Five million francs.
Nobody speaks. The car is very quiet. Outside, the traffic continues: horns, motorbikes, a woman selling water bags shouting "Eau glacée! Eau glacée!"
Awa thinks.
With five million francs, she can pay the school fees. Not only this year: all the years. High school. University. Medical school.
With five million francs, her father can buy a new taxi. A good one. Or two taxis.
With five million francs, they can pay Bakary, pay the rent, buy football shoes for Ismaël, a new stall at the market for her mother.
Nobody knows. The young man didn't look at the taxi. He didn't see the number. Abidjan has thousands of orange taxis.
She looks at the money. Then she looks at her father.
He is not looking at the money. He is looking at her. Waiting.
"What do we do, Awa?" he asks softly.
Awa remembers many things in one second.
She remembers Zié and his gold teeth. *Many people think he is clever.*
She remembers her father's words: *A man must be able to sleep at night.*
She remembers Aminata, the nurse, smiling after twelve hours of work.
She remembers Mama Akissi, who brings a chicken every week to her daughter, because love is something you give, not something you take.
And she thinks: if I become a doctor with this money, what kind of doctor will I be?
Awa takes a deep breath.
"We give it back, Papa. It isn't ours."
Her father closes his eyes for a moment. When he opens them, there are tears in them. And he smiles. It is the biggest smile she has ever seen on his face.
"That's my daughter," he says. "That's my doctor."
He closes the envelope and puts it carefully back in the bag.
"Now," he says, "we have to find him."
They look in the bag again, slowly this time. In a small pocket, there is a business card.
*Kouamé Yao — Director — KY Construction — Riviera 3, Abidjan.*
"It must be his father," says Awa. "On the phone, he said 'Papa'."
"Riviera 3," says her father. "Let's go."
They drive across Cocody. Her father drives carefully, with both hands on the wheel. Awa holds the bag on her knees. She feels like she is carrying a bomb.
Riviera 3 is a quiet neighbourhood with big houses, high walls and trees. They find the building: a large white office with blue windows. Above the door, big letters: *KY CONSTRUCTION*.
A guard stands at the gate. He is wearing a uniform and sunglasses. He looks at the orange taxi with disgust.
"Taxi drivers wait outside," he says. "No entry."
"We want to see Monsieur Kouamé," says her father politely. "It's important."
"Monsieur Kouamé is busy. Do you have an appointment?"
"No, but —"
"No appointment, no entry." The guard turns his back.
Her father looks at Awa. He is not used to these big buildings, these men in uniforms who look at him like he is nothing. He wants to leave the bag with the guard and go.
But Awa does not give up. She gets out of the taxi and walks to the guard.
"Sir," she says, loud and clear, like when she shouts "Adjamé! Plateau!". "Please tell Monsieur Kouamé that we have his son's black bag. With the envelope inside."
The guard turns around. He takes off his sunglasses. He looks at the bag. Then he takes his radio.
Five minutes later, a young man runs down the stairs of the building. It is the young man from the taxi! His shirt is open, his face is grey with fear.
"My bag! Where did you find it? Is everything there? Is the envelope there?"
"Everything is there," says Awa. "We didn't take anything."
He opens the bag with shaking hands. He takes out the envelope. He counts the bundles, once, twice. Then he sits down on the stairs and puts his head in his hands.
"Ten," he says. "All ten. Oh my God. Thank you. Thank you."
His name is Serge. He is not the director. He is the director's son, and he works for his father.

"It's the money for the workers' salaries," he explains. "Fifty workers on our building site in Bingerville. They are waiting for their pay today. If the money was lost..." He shakes his head. "My father would kill me. And fifty families would have nothing this month."
Then an older man comes down the stairs. He is tall, with grey hair and a dark suit. He walks slowly, like a man who is used to being listened to.
"Serge," he says. Only that one word. But Serge stands up immediately.
"Papa, they found the bag. Everything is there."
Monsieur Kouamé looks at the bag. Then he looks at Moussa, in his old shirt. And at Awa, in her school uniform skirt and her flip-flops. And at the orange taxi behind the gate, with its dented door.
He doesn't smile. He doesn't say thank you.
"Come inside," he says. "Both of you. I want to understand this story."
Awa looks at her father. Her father looks at her. Something in Monsieur Kouamé's voice makes them nervous.
They follow him up the stairs.
Monsieur Kouamé's office is enormous. There is cold air conditioning, a big wooden desk, and a window with a view of the lagoon. On the wall, there are photos of bridges, buildings and roads.
He sits behind the desk. He doesn't offer them a chair, so Awa and her father stand.
"Serge," he says. "Count it again. In front of me."
Serge puts the bundles on the desk. He takes off the rubber bands. He counts the notes, one by one. It takes a long time. Nobody speaks. Awa can hear the air conditioning and her own heart.
Finally, Serge stops. His face changes.
"Papa... there are only nine bundles of five hundred thousand. And one bundle is... it's only four hundred thousand. A hundred thousand francs are missing."
Monsieur Kouamé turns his eyes to Moussa. They are cold eyes.

"A hundred thousand francs," he says slowly. "Interesting. You bring back four million nine hundred thousand francs, and you keep a small part for yourself. Clever. Nobody notices a hundred thousand in five million. Is that it?"
Awa feels the blood rush to her face.
"No! We didn't take anything! I counted it in the taxi, my father counted it, everything was there!"
"Then where are the hundred thousand francs, young lady?"
Her father puts his hand on her shoulder. His voice is calm, but Awa can feel his hand shaking.
"Monsieur, I have driven a taxi for twelve years in Abidjan. Thousands of passengers. Phones, wallets, bags. I have always given everything back. Everything. Ask anyone in Abobo."
"I don't know anyone in Abobo," says Monsieur Kouamé.
He picks up the phone on his desk. "I will call the police. They will search your taxi. If the money is not there, you can go."

Awa's legs become weak. The police. In Abidjan, everybody knows what can happen with the police. Her father could spend the night in a cell. They could take the taxi. They could ask for money. And everybody in the neighbourhood would say: Moussa Traoré, the thief.
Then Awa remembers something.
"Wait!" she says. "Please wait, Monsieur. One minute."
She takes her green notebook out of her pocket. She opens it at today's page. Her hands are shaking, but her voice is clear.

"I write everything in the taxi. Look. Today, 2:40 p.m., Adjamé. Young man, well dressed, black bag, talks on the phone in French and English. He said: *Yes, Papa, I have the money for the workers. No, I'm not late.*" She looks at Serge. "And before that, he said something else. I wrote it because I thought it was strange."
She reads:
*"Don't worry, Didier, I'll give you your hundred when I see you tonight. Yes, from the envelope. My father will never know."*
The office is completely silent.
Monsieur Kouamé slowly puts the phone down. He turns his head towards his son.
"Serge," he says. "Who is Didier?"
Serge's face is now very pale. He opens his mouth. He closes it.
"Papa, I... I can explain."
"Then explain."

"Didier is a friend. I owed him money. A bet on a football match. I took a hundred thousand this morning, before going to the bank. I wanted to put it back next week, from my salary. Nobody would know..." He looks at the floor. "I'm sorry."
Monsieur Kouamé doesn't shout. That is worse. He looks at his son for a long, long time. Then he says, very quietly:
"A taxi driver from Abobo, who has nothing, found five million francs and brought back every franc. And my son, who has everything, steals from fifty workers to pay a bet."
Serge says nothing. There is nothing to say.
Monsieur Kouamé stands up. He walks around the desk. He stops in front of Moussa. And then he does something nobody expects.
He bows his head.
"Monsieur Traoré," he says. "I insulted you. In front of your daughter. I am ashamed. Please forgive me."
Monsieur Kouamé asks for chairs. He asks for cold drinks. A secretary brings bottles of bissap and a plate of biscuits. Awa is so nervous that she can't eat, but she drinks the bissap in one go.

Serge has left the room. His father sent him to Bingerville with the money for the workers. "You will give the money to each worker yourself," he told him. "And you will look at each one of them in the eyes."
Now Monsieur Kouamé sits in front of Moussa and Awa. Not behind his desk. In front of them, on a chair, like a normal man.
"Tell me about yourselves," he says.
So her father talks. About Abobo. About twelve years of driving. About the orange taxi, the breakdown, Bakary's garage, the debt. He doesn't complain; he just tells the facts.
Then Monsieur Kouamé turns to Awa. "And the notebook? Why do you write the passengers' stories?"
Awa explains. About wanting to be a doctor. About Aminata the nurse. About listening to people, not only looking at them.
"And the school fees?" he asks. "Your father said your school has a deadline."
Awa looks at her father. He says nothing. So she tells the truth. "Sixty-five thousand francs. By Friday. We have thirty-one."
Monsieur Kouamé is quiet for a moment. He looks at the photos of bridges on his wall.

"I started with nothing, you know," he says. "My father was a mason in Daloa. I carried cement bags on building sites when I was sixteen. Somebody gave me a chance once. An old Lebanese engineer. He paid for my studies because he said I asked good questions." He smiles for the first time. "I think you ask good questions too, Awa."
He takes a piece of paper and a pen.

"Here is what I propose. First, Monsieur Traoré: my company needs a driver for our new minibus. We transport workers every day from Abobo and Yopougon to our building sites. A good salary, every month. Health insurance for your family. A new vehicle. And Sundays free."
Her father doesn't move.

"Second: KY Construction has a scholarship fund for good students from poor families. It pays school fees until the *baccalauréat*. And if the student continues to have good results, it pays for university. Awa, bring me your school results on Monday."
Awa's heart is beating so fast that she thinks everybody can hear it.
But her father stands up.
"Thank you, Monsieur Kouamé," he says slowly. "You are very generous. But I cannot accept."
Awa turns to him, shocked. "Papa!"

"We didn't bring back the bag to get a reward," he continues. "We brought it back because it was the right thing to do. If I accept your job and your money now, people will say I was paid for my honesty. And then what is my honesty worth?" He shakes his head. "My father taught me: when you do good, don't hold out your hand."
Monsieur Kouamé looks at him with deep respect.

"Monsieur Traoré, I understand your pride. I respect it. But listen to me. This is not a reward. Today you showed me that you are honest. My son showed me that he is not — yet. I need honest men in my company. It's not a gift. It's a job. You will work hard for it."
Her father hesitates.
Then Awa speaks. Her voice is small, but firm.

"Papa. You always say a man must be able to sleep at night. If you say no, I don't think any of us will sleep tonight. And it's not charity. You heard him: it's work. And the scholarship... I will work for it too. I promise. Every day."
Her father looks at her for a long time. At his daughter, in her school skirt and flip-flops, with her green notebook in her hand.
Then he sits down again. He holds out his hand — not to ask, but to shake.
"OK," he says to Monsieur Kouamé. "But I keep my orange taxi. For Sundays."
Monsieur Kouamé laughs, a big, surprising laugh. He shakes Moussa's hand.
"Deal."

On the way home, the old orange taxi coughs more than ever. Vroom, cough, cough, vroom. But nobody cares. Awa and her father sing loudly with the radio, an old song by Magic System. They sing so badly that a policeman at a roundabout laughs and waves them on without stopping them.

At home, her mother is cooking. When she hears the story, she sits down on the kitchen stool and cries. Then she laughs. Then she cries again. Ismaël doesn't understand everything, but he dances around the mango tree shouting, "We are rich! We are rich!"
"We are not rich," says her father, smiling. "We are lucky. And we will work."
That night, everybody sleeps very, very well.
On Monday, Awa brings her school results to KY Construction. On Tuesday, Madame Koné calls her into her office again.

"Awa, I received a letter from a company called KY Construction. Your school fees are paid. For this year and the next three years." She looks at Awa over her glasses. "Do you want to tell me what happened?"
So Awa tells her. Madame Koné listens without interrupting. At the end, she takes off her glasses and wipes her eyes.
"In thirty years of teaching," she says, "this is the best story I have heard. Now go and study. You have an exam in six weeks, and your last maths mark was eleven."
Six weeks. The BEPC, the big national exam at the end of *troisième*. Every student in Côte d'Ivoire is afraid of it.

Awa studies like never before. In the morning before school. In the evening after school. On Saturdays, she doesn't go in the taxi anymore — her father drives the new white minibus now, from Monday to Friday, and on Saturday he says: "You study. That's your taxi now."
But mathematics is difficult. Equations, geometry, problems with trains that leave at different times. Some nights, Awa cries over her exercise book.
One evening, she remembers the small piece of paper. Aminata's number.
She hesitates for a long time. Then she sends a message.
*Hello, it's Awa, the girl from the orange taxi. I have the BEPC in four weeks and I'm lost in maths. Sorry to disturb you.*
The answer arrives ten minutes later.
*Awa! Of course I remember you. You don't disturb me. I'm free on Sunday afternoon. I was very good in maths, you know. Come to the hospital café at 3pm.*

So every Sunday afternoon, Awa takes the bus to Cocody. In the small café of the children's hospital, between two shifts, Aminata explains equations on paper napkins. She is patient. She draws pictures. She makes jokes about trains.
"Why do these trains always leave at the same time?" she says. "In Abidjan, no train is ever on time!"
Sometimes, between two exercises, Aminata takes Awa to the corridor. Through the windows, Awa sees the little rooms, the children in their beds, the doctors in white coats.
"That's why you study maths," says Aminata. "One day, you will calculate a medicine dose for a baby. You can't make a mistake. Every number is a life."
After that, Awa never complains about equations again.
The day of the exam arrives. Awa wakes up at four o'clock. She can't sleep anymore.
At five o'clock, she hears a sound in front of the house. Vroom, vroom, cough, cough.
She runs outside. Her father is sitting in the old orange taxi, the engine running, the light on.
"Get in, doctor," he says. "Today, I'm your driver."
He drives her to the exam centre. Before she gets out, he gives her a small paper bag. Inside, there is a pen. A new, beautiful blue pen.
"From all the passengers," he says with a wink. "Mama Akissi, Kader, the man with two phones. Everybody says: good luck."
Awa laughs. Then she walks into the exam centre, her new pen in her hand, her head full of trains and equations and children in hospital beds.
The results of the BEPC arrive one month later, on a hot morning in July.
The whole neighbourhood is waiting. In Abobo, results day is like a football final. Families gather around radios and phones. Children run from house to house with the news.
Awa can't look. She gives her phone to Ismaël. "You look. I can't."
Ismaël reads slowly, his finger on the screen. "Traoré Awa... ad... admis... admise... with... mention... *très bien*?" He looks up. "What is *très bien*?"

Her mother screams. Her father picks Awa up and turns her around in the courtyard like when she was a little girl. The neighbours come running. Somebody puts on music. Mama Fanta from next door brings a huge plate of alloco. By noon, there is a party under the mango tree.
In the evening, Awa sends three messages.
To Aminata: *Mention très bien. In maths: 16/20. The trains arrived on time.*
To Madame Koné: *Thank you for believing in me.*
To Monsieur Kouamé: *I passed. I will continue to work hard. Please say thank you to Serge too. Without his mistake, none of this would have happened.*

The answer from Monsieur Kouamé arrives the next morning. It's a photo. Serge, in a yellow helmet, on the building site in Bingerville, carrying bags of cement with the workers. Under the photo, a message:
*He is learning. Like me at sixteen. Congratulations, doctor.*
Years pass.

Awa goes to high school, then to the *Lycée scientifique* in Yamoussoukro. She comes home every holiday. Every Sunday, wherever she is, she writes in her green notebook — now it's her fifth green notebook. Ismaël grows tall and plays football for the youth team of a club in Abobo. Her mother opens a bigger stall at the market, with a sign: *Pagnes Mariam — Quality and Honesty*.

Her father drives the white minibus for KY Construction. He is now the head of all the drivers. He has trained twelve young men. The first lesson he gives them is always the same: "A good driver brings everybody home. And he must be able to sleep at night."
On Sundays, he still takes out the old orange taxi. Not for money. Just to drive around Abobo, say hello to everybody, and give free rides to the old women going to church.
Zié sold his three taxis. Nobody knows where he went.
Six years after the day of the black bag, Awa Traoré starts her first year of medicine at the University Félix Houphouët-Boigny in Cocody.
On the first morning, at six o'clock, a sound wakes up the whole street. Vroom, vroom, cough, cough.
The orange taxi is in front of the house. It is very old now. One door is a different colour. The radio doesn't work anymore. But it starts.
"Get in, doctor," says her father.

They drive across Abidjan in the early morning. Adjamé. Plateau. The bridges over the lagoon, shining in the sun — new bridges, built by engineers like Kader. Cocody, and the big children's hospital where Aminata is now the head nurse.
In front of the university, her father stops the car. He doesn't say anything. He just looks at her, his eyes wet.
Awa notices something new on the back window of the taxi. A small sticker, white with blue letters. Her father put it there himself.
It says: *Honest roads lead far.*
That night, in her new room at the university, Awa opens her green notebook at a new page. She thinks for a long time. Then she writes:

*Today I learned what I already knew in the taxi.*
*Every passenger has a story.*
*And our story is written by the choices we make —*
*especially the ones nobody else will ever see.*
She closes the notebook. Somewhere in Abidjan, an old orange taxi is coughing its way home.
— The End —

title: The Taxi Driver's Daughter
author: Léxi
desc: Awa, 15 ans, aide son père chauffeur de woro-woro à Abidjan. Un jour, elle trouve cinq millions de francs sur la banquette arrière… Roman complet.
